Header: Oidium mangiferae Amharic: amedaye; Tigrigna: hammokshtay; Oromifa: dakuya

Prevention: Use resistant varieties and ensure transplanting of seedlings free from powdery mildew disease
Plant at proper spacing usually 6m x 6m (but this will depend on the variety)
Carry out regular pruning of tree branches, this allow good air circulation reduces humidity in the canpoy that favors the establishment, development and reproduction of the pathogen
Pick up fallen leaves and flowers and bury 60cm deep as these can harbour the fungus and help spread the disease
Use clean pruning equipment to avoid contamination, use fire to sterilise
In nurseries, avoid overhead watering to reduce the relative humidity as excessive watering increases the incidence of the disease
Minimize movement from infected to disease free fields
Monitoring: Before blossoming, mark 5 trees/ha randomly in orchard and check for symptoms of the disease each week:
Young infected leaves develop grey necrotic lesions on the upper side of leaves and tend to curl downwards - If severe, the leaves may become brown, dry and fall
Flowers fail to open, blacken or become brown and dry and may fall from panicles as they become completely covered by the fungus - A severe blossom infection can result in complete loss of fruit
If young fruit is infected the skin cracks becomes corky, this may cover the entire fruit
Carry out control measures when 5% symptoms severity is observed
Direct Control: Carry out phytosanitary pruning by removing all infected twigs, branches and panicles.
Destroy these by burning or bury 60cm deep.
Do not compost infected plant debris
Spray infected shoots with a solution of 6 spoons of baking powder, 3 spoons of white oil and white bar soap foam and
Mix in 15 litres of water and spray every week to reduce infection
Restrictions: There are no registered fungicides in
Ethiopia for the management of powdery mildew on mango.
